To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are polynomial-time approximation algorithms for a number of combinatorial problems for which the ratio of the best solution value that can possibly be chosen by the algorithms to the optimum value is bounded by a small constant, independent of problem size, and that there is a problem for which no algorithm with a worst case performance ratio of less than 0(n) is known.
for certain optimization problems, there are simple algorithms for which the worst case ratio is constant, and for other problems there are no such algorithms.

there are problems for which there are simple polynomial time heuristic algorithms that find solutions whose value is at most a constant times optimal; that there are problems that have simple polynomial time algorithms whose worst case ratio grows with the problem size; and that there are problems whose optimal solution value cannot be approximated by any polynomial time algorithm to within a factor of 0(nò), where nò is the problem size
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and analysis of simple, efficient algorithms for finding approximate, polynomial time solutions to NP-complete optimization problems.
the design and analysis of simple approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems.
the design and analysis of approximation algorithms for combinatorially hard problems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for many problems of combinatorial optimization, there are simple algorithms that yield solutions whose quality is bounded by a small constant factor.

, for a wide range of problems, simple polynomial-time algorithms exist that yield solutions whose value is within a constant factor of optimal, and for a wide range, no such algorithm has been found.
the ratio of worst case solution values to optimal values for the algorithms considered grows with the log of n for some problems, with n for other problems, and is constant for still other problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the simple algorithms are surprisingly good.
the worst case performance of these algorithms can be quite bad, but that there are problems for which good approximation algorithms can be found.

, in general, it seems difficult to find polynomial-time algorithms for which the worst case performance ratio does not grow with the problem size, and that the problem of finding such algorithms is a difficult one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a wide range of problem classes for which there exist polynomial time approximation algorithms that yield good solutions.
, for a wide variety of optimization problems, there is no algorithm which can guarantee a worst case performance ratio of less than a constant, no matter what the problem size.
, for certain classes of combinatorial problems, there exist polynomial-time algorithms that yield approximate solutions with guaranteed performance bounds.
